body_markdown:
Every October, Maire Anne and I have a long history of going up to Manchester, Vermont, to visit dear friends. In addition to catching up on a 40-plus-year-long relationship, playing music with a former bandmate, and geeking out on the spectacular fall foliage, it’s an opportunity to take one of the fun cars on a mini road trip. While the 300-mile round trip is a blink compared with my 2000-mile annual haul to and from The Vintage in Asheville, I didn’t make it down there this year, so I was a little road-trip itchy.


The annual Manchester-trip question always is: Which fun car should I take? Most of the Hagerty-insured cars have done the annual Vermont excursion, including the[’73 E9 3.0CSi coupe](https://bimmerlife.com/2021/10/09/rene-and-i-head-to-saratoga/) , the Bavaria, the[Euro 635CSi](https://bimmerlife.com/2024/10/16/shark-sighted-in-vermont/) , and[Hampton the survivor ’73 2002](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/the-low-mileage-car-gets-a-road-trip/) . Last year, for a number of reasons, we exercised the safe choice and took Maire Anne’s[Honda Fit](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/pre-road-trip-surprises/) , so this year I felt honor-bound to nudge the dial a bit in the visceral direction. But not too far. When traveling with my wife, it’s appropriate to calibrate the degree of “adventure” accordingly.


As it happened, all three of my red cars—the 3.0CSi, the Lotus Elan +2, and the FrankenThirty (the salvaged-titled BMW E30 that’s two-thirds 1988 325is and one-third 1987 325e) were here at the house. The 3.0 is *always* here; I don’t store it anywhere else. The Elan +2 has been here since I bought it two years ago. But after I[used the FrankenThirty to make the trip to The Vintage in 2024](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/road-tripping-the-frankenthirty/) , it spent much of the time in storage in Monson.


It was red car central at Chez Hack.


Rob Siegel


In early July, I brought the M Coupe and the FrankenThirty back from Monson—the former to sell, and the latter to just have around. I’ve grown to enjoy the ratty E30 for the friendly, just-glad-to-be-part-of-the-family mongrel that it is. For some crazy reason, when the car was rebuilt from its salvage event in 1990, the 121-hp “e” engine was installed in it, so it has 47 fewer horsepower than the “i” engine it’s supposed to have, but it has a few more foot-pounds of torque, so it moves out of its own way just fine. It also handles well, and with the gold BBS basketweaves I installed on it, it’s kind of a rolling 1980s BMW joke that makes me laugh whenever I look at it.


It’s my “I’m 28 years old, I’m pulling down $200K at Lehman Brothers, and I’m about to enter rehab” car.


Rob Siegel


So, which red vintage car to take? Tough choices when you’re down from 14 to 10 cars, huh?


The answer was actually pretty easy: If the forecast showed zero rain, the 3.0CSi would get the nod. If there was just a little rain forecast, the Lotus Elan +2 would step out, Lucas electricals be damned. But if the weather-media powers that be were predicting a drenching, the FrankenThirty would take the soaking for the team.


As the weekend approached, the forecast was looking wet, so the keep-dry E9 coupe stayed indoors. I really wanted to take the Elan +2, as other than a[day trip to New Hampshire last year](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/completing-the-circle-with-the-lotus-elan-2/https:/www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/the-hack-mechanic/completing-the-circle-with-the-lotus-elan-2/) , the car hasn’t had a real road trip, but two things stayed my hand. The first was that, as I mentioned a few weeks ago, I’ve been playing Whack-a-Mole with a few reliability issues, and I’m not completely certain I’ve driven the little buggers deep enough into their dens. But the other is that Maire Anne has ridden short distances with me in the Elan +2 a few times, and the combination of its low floor, which makes entry complicated, the seating position, the throaty exhaust, and the sharp smell of unburned hydrocarbons doesn’t make it a comfortable ride for her.


So the FrankenThirty it was.


Make no mistake, I had concerns about *it,* too. After I bought the car two years ago, I did a pretty thorough job resurrecting it and sorting it out before driving it to The Vintage the following spring. On that road trip, the main issue was surprisingly high oil consumption—like a quart every 500 miles. Since then, I replaced the alternator when it quit charging, and… that’s about it.


But I always think about “The Big Seven” reasons cars, particularly old ones, die on road trips (ignition, fuel delivery, cooling, charging, belts, clutch hydraulics, and make sure to check the ball joints ‘cause if they break, you lose control of the car). This is a modern-enough car that it has Motronic engine management, so ignition-wise, there’s basically nothing to do unless the crank sensor craps out. I’d replaced the fuel filter and any cracked fuel lines two years ago but left the working fuel pump alone. I gave the cooling system what it needed, but didn’t replace everything. The belts were all new. I hadn’t replaced the clutch slave or master cylinder because I haven’t seen the spate of clutch hydraulic failures on 1980s BMWs that I’ve seen on 1970s BMWs, at least not yet. And the ball joints were new.


So sort of a mixed bag, right?


I put the car up on ramps, saw the attendant oil and power steering wetness that most non-concours cars have, drove it, experienced only the groaning of the power steering pump when it was cold, and called it good enough for a 300-mile trip with my wife.


Rob Siegel


Since the drive to Manchester was only 150 miles each way (within my Hagerty Drivers Club towing radius!) I elected to pack light—my road toolbox, spare belts, a length of fuel line, a battery jump pack, a quart of oil, and that was it. No floor jack and stands, no gallon of antifreeze. I did bring a pint of brake fluid and a spare 90-degree ¼-inch barbed connector, as when I resurrected the car, I cut the end off the swelled and leaking line from the reservoir down to the clutch master and spliced in a connector and short hose, so I wanted to be prepared if the connector broke.


The FrankenThirty’s Motronic injection system and working catalytic converter don’t pump out the acrid, eye-watering fumes that a carbureted car does (a rich-running de-catted vintage car can do this, too), but the car *does* have some residual contamination from the mouse issues it had when I bought it. Even though I cleaned the heater box and scrubbed the heater and evaporator cores, it can still be a little fragrant, and Maire Anne has a very sensitive sense of smell. I gave her veto power, but she left it up to me. I drove the car quite a bit in the week prior to leaving. With passive vent air on, it was fine. With the A/C on, the smell was barely perceptible. But with the heat on, it was right on the line. I took the car for a 40-mile drive with the windows down and the heat blasting to try to cook off whatever was offensive, and hoped for the best.


That Saturday, Maire Anne and I packed the FrankenThirty with rainy-weather clothes, a cool metal-bodied resonator guitar I’d recently bought, an apple pie she’d just baked, a few bottles of wine, what was left of a bottle of Lagavulin, and a few changes of clothes, and headed north.


Maire Anne and I wearing our Vermont autumn colors.


Rob Siegel


Manchester is nestled in the Green Mountains, and it’s a lovely drive. One of the quirks of the long, thin state that is Vermont is that if your destination isn’t on due-north-south-and-barely-west-of-New-Hampshire I-90 or on oblique-oriented I-89, then you’ll be driving mostly on local roads. As such, it takes us about the same three-and-a-quarter hours to knock off the 150 miles to Manchester that it does to head the 225 miles up I-89 to Burlington. But I’m not complaining. The sun was out, the traffic was light, and the trees were turning. It was perfect. On road trips, I often think of the country song “Looking at the World Through a Windshield.” It was a lovely world.


Command Cody and Dell Reeves would’ve approved.


Rob Siegel


By the time we got to Manchester, the colors were spectacular. There are two things in this world that are never overrated: The Grand Canyon, and New England foliage.


Yeah baby. Too bad your photographer can’t properly place a car relative to a tree.


Rob Siegel


Two wonderful dinners followed by two sessions of guitar playing and scotch drinking, and it was over. Incredibly, most of the forecast rain came overnight. When we left on Monday morning and headed out of Manchester under the shadow of Bromley Mountain, the visibility suddenly dropped to less than a hundred feet


And miles to go before we sleep.


Rob Siegel


Fortunately, within ten miles, the fog was behind us, the sun came out, and it was back to fall’s magical show.


Oh, you want to know how the FrankenThirty did? Worst road trip to write a vintage car article about ever. Nothing went wrong. The only thing of note was a bit of front-end shudder on braking that reminded me that, when I replaced the lower control arms two years ago, I reused the “lollypop” bushings that mount them to the frame. I bought them after I got back from The Vintage with the intent of installing them before the next road trip and had forgotten all about the issue. Other than that, the car did great. Due to tourists like us leaf-peeping on this holiday weekend, I didn’t have much chance to carve corners on empty roads, but I don’t do much of that with Maire Anne in the car anyway. And I never had to turn on the heat, so Maire Anne never complained about the smell.


So, here’s to fun cars, tolerant spouses, compliant cars, and old friends who live exactly the right distance away.


***
